definition: Opportunistic reasoning is a method of selecting a suitable logical inference strategy within artificial intelligence applications.
details: Specific reasoning methods may be used to draw conclusions from a set of given facts in a knowledge base, e.g. forward chaining versus backward chaining. However, in opportunistic reasoning, pieces of knowledge may be applied either forward or backward, at the "most opportune time". An opportunistic reasoning system may combine elements of both forward and backward reasoning. It is useful when the number of possible inferences is very large and the reasoning system must be responsive to new data that may become known. Opportunistic reasoning has been used in applications such as blackboard systems and medical applications.

explainer.lead: Opportunistic reasoning is a way of choosing which inference strategy to apply in an AI system. It matters when the space of possible inferences is huge and the system must react to new data.

tiers.eli5: Instead of always solving a puzzle one fixed way, the system picks whichever move looks best at that moment, forward or backward.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it in knowledge-based systems to apply rules forward or backward at the most opportune time, mixing both styles. A pitfall is the added control complexity needed to decide opportunistically, which can be harder to debug than a fixed strategy.
tiers.paperLevel: In opportunistic reasoning, pieces of knowledge may be applied either forward or backward, at the most opportune time; systems may combine forward and backward chaining. It suits cases where the number of possible inferences is very large.

explainer.example: A diagnostic system starts backward from a hypothesis, then switches to forward chaining when a new sensor fact arrives that suggests a different cause.
